claims.paraphrase: The specification assigns model-theoretic truth conditions to RDF graphs and RDF/RDFS vocabularies, characterizing truth-preserving transformations and derivations.
Passages are normative except sections explicitly marked non-normative and authoring guidelines, diagrams, examples and notes.
Capitalized requirement keywords have their RFC 2119 meanings.
Normative authority concerns RDF semantics and inference validity; social naming conventions and relationships to non-RDF Web content are outside the specified semantics.
Additional semantic assumptions about an RDF vocabulary constitute a semantic extension and determine an entailment regime.
Extensions may restrict legal graph syntax and treat violations as errors; none of the extensions normatively defined here adds such graph restrictions.
Whenever G simply entails H, every extension must preserve that entailment if its additional syntactic conditions hold; stronger semantics cannot cancel an accepted simple entailment.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: Restricting simple interpretations by conditions C preserves every simple entailment and every SimplyValid process.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: C retains the same Satisfies relation and graph syntax. The source also permits separate syntactic admissibility conditions, not represented by C; their satisfaction remains a separate obligation.

claims.paraphrase: IRI, triple, graph, subject, predicate, object, RDF source, node, blank node, literal, graph isomorphism and dataset have their Concepts meanings.
An RDF graph is a set of RDF triples, using RDF-term identity for its triple components.
claims.formalization_note: A list implementation may represent a graph through its membership set; this definition alone does not establish a unique enumeration or a correct cardinality operation.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: An RDF graph G is a set of RDF triples; equality of G is equality of membership.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Concepts supplies the term domains; their concrete lexical constraints remain open.

claims.paraphrase: An ordinary RDF triple has an IRI or blank-node subject, an IRI predicate, and an IRI, blank-node or literal object; those term kinds are distinct.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: An ordinary RDF triple has subject in IRI or Blank, predicate in IRI, and object in IRI or Literal or Blank.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Disjoint syntactic categories are enforced. IRI and Literal are abstract domains, not validated concrete strings.

claims.paraphrase: Abstract IRI and literal identity follow Concepts, not equality of denoted values; blank-node identifiers are concrete-syntax labels rather than the abstract blank nodes themselves.
claims.formalization_note: Check literal language-tag identity against Concepts separately from the lowercase language-tag value condition in section 7.1.

claims.paraphrase: All definitions apply unchanged to generalized triples, graphs and datasets, whose triple positions can each contain any RDF term.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: A generalized triple permits any RDF term in each of its three positions; a generalized graph is a set of generalized triples.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Ordinary graphs embed into generalized graphs. Instance and interpolation claims for generalized syntax have not been discharged.

claims.paraphrase: An interpretation maps IRIs and literals into a semantic domain subject to constraints; qualified kinds of interpretation determine corresponding entailment regimes.

Denoting and referring name the interpretation-dependent relationship to a referent; identifying denotes an externally established naming relationship, which need not agree with a particular interpretation.
Equality denotes strict identity, and angle-bracket pairs are ordered pairs; these conventions apply throughout the mathematics.
A name is an IRI or literal; a typed literal contributes itself and its datatype IRI as names, and a vocabulary is a set of names.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: Name is Iri or Literal. Term.names includes a literal itself and its syntactic datatype IRI; a graph vocabulary is the union of the names contributed by its terms.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: The total datatype : Literal → Iri projection is an explicit interface parameter. Concrete literal syntax, identity, lexical constraints and correctness of the supplied projection remain external obligations.

claims.paraphrase: The empty graph is the empty set of triples.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: The empty graph contains no triples.

claims.paraphrase: Subgraphs and proper subgraphs are respectively subsets and proper subsets of triples; a triple is identified with its singleton subgraph.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: H is a subgraph of G exactly when every member of H is a member of G.

claims.paraphrase: A ground graph has no blank nodes.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: G is ground exactly when no blank node occurs in any triple of G.

claims.paraphrase: An instance is obtained by consistently replacing some or all blank nodes through a function into RDF terms; names already in the graph are unchanged.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: H is an IsInstance of G exactly when one partial Substitution μ replaces each selected blank consistently, leaving omitted blanks and all names fixed, and H is the set of resulting triples.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Shared ambient blank identities; the generalized syntax admits substitutions in every position. Use ordinary Graph endpoints when ordinary RDF syntax is required.

claims.paraphrase: Instantiation is reflexive and composes transitively; every resulting triple is an instance of at least one original triple.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: IsInstance is reflexive and transitive. For a fixed μ, every triple in G.substitute μ is the image of a triple in G.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: No finiteness or injectivity assumption; different triples may have the same image.

claims.paraphrase: An instance relative to vocabulary V uses only names in V for substituted names; substitutions by blank nodes are still permitted.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: InstanceWithVocabulary V H G requires an instance mapping whose name-valued replacements of occurring blanks lie in V; existing names need not lie in V.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: V is a set of IRI-or-literal names, represented by Sum Iri Literal.

claims.paraphrase: An instance is proper if some blank node becomes a name or distinct blank nodes are identified by the substitution.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: ProperInstance H G has an instance mapping that replaces an occurring blank by a name, or maps two distinct occurring blanks to the same resolved term.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Only blanks occurring in G count; omitted replacements resolve to the unchanged blank. Proper instance does not mean proper subgraph.

claims.paraphrase: Graph isomorphism is an invertible renaming of blank nodes, leaving names fixed; isomorphic graphs are mutual instances and may be treated as identical up to that renaming.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: GraphIsomorphism G H supplies inverse blank renamings on the occurring blank nodes and a graph-image equality. The graphs are mutual instances and satisfy exactly the same simple interpretations.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: A common ambient identity domain; unused identities need not be bijective. Isomorphism does not assert literal set equality or preservation of blank sharing with other graphs. A separately packaged Concepts bijection over all graph nodes remains to be provided.

claims.paraphrase: A graph is lean if none of its instances is a proper subgraph of itself.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: LeanGraph G means that every instance H of G that is a subgraph of G equals G: no instance is a proper subgraph.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Lean here is the RDF mathematical property, unrelated to the name of the proof assistant.

claims.paraphrase: A non-lean graph is logically redundant relative to its lean subgraphs; every ground graph is lean.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: Every ground G is a LeanGraph. For ordinary graphs G and H, if H is both an instance and a subgraph of G, the graphs are LogicallyEquivalent.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Does not prove existence of lean subgraphs, or the source’s entire informal redundancy discussion; no generalized instance theorem is assumed.

claims.paraphrase: Repeated occurrences of the identical triple do not add graph members, and order does not distinguish graphs with the same members.
claims.formalization_note: This is the mathematical consequence of sethood, not a separately coded entailment rule or a requirement to reject duplicate surface-syntax statements.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: For every set G, G union G equals G; repeated occurrences of a triple in an input list denote the same set as one occurrence.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: This is a mathematical consequence of the set definition, not a separately labelled W3C rule.

claims.paraphrase: Blank-node sharing between graphs requires a source structure that provides for shared identity; repeated retrieval of the same document or source does not by itself identify its blank nodes.
Applications manipulating scoped blank-node labels should track the abstract identities and rename labels when combining sources to prevent accidental conflation.
claims.formalization_note: This is an authoring/implementation guideline under the section 2 exception, not a new truth condition.

claims.paraphrase: Graph union uses triple-set union and preserves actual blank-node identities, including identities shared across inputs.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: The union of G and H contains a triple exactly when G or H contains that triple, preserving blank-node identity.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Binary union; arbitrary families are not yet implemented.

claims.paraphrase: Merge first separates blank nodes shared between inputs, then takes their union; merging subgraphs can therefore produce a larger graph.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: The binary merge of G and H takes their union after placing their blank nodes in disjoint copies. I satisfies that merge exactly when I satisfies G and I satisfies H.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Uses Sum B₁ B₂ for fresh identities. This is a representative up to blank-node renaming; literal equality to union for already-disjoint domains is not asserted.

claims.paraphrase: The union is an instance of the merge; when inputs share no blank nodes, union and merge coincide. Union retains the joint content, including shared blank-node meaning.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: For any G and H with a common blank-node domain, their union simply entails their merge.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Semantic consequence only. The stated syntactic instance relation and no-shared-nodes equality remain open.

claims.paraphrase: All semantic extensions must preserve the simple truth conditions; they may add constraints but must not modify or negate those conditions.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: For an extension represented by additional conditions C on simple interpretations, simple entailment implies entailment under C.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Models only extensions over this graph syntax; does not formalize every permitted higher-level notation.

claims.paraphrase: Semantics applies to a graph rather than a changing RDF source; a source is interpreted through its graph value at a time or state, while a fixed graph does not change meaning with time.
A simple interpretation includes a nonempty resource set IR.
claims.source_locator: Definition of a simple interpretation, numbered component 1

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: IR is a nonempty set of resources.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: IR and IP are predicates on an ambient type U; no finiteness assumption.

claims.paraphrase: A simple interpretation includes a property set IP.
claims.source_locator: Definition of a simple interpretation, numbered component 2

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: IP is a set of properties, permitted to overlap IR.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: No IP subset IR constraint is imposed in simple interpretations.

claims.paraphrase: IEXT maps each element of IP to a subset of IR × IR; this set of pairs is the property extension.
claims.source_locator: Definition of a simple interpretation, numbered component 3

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: For every p in IP, IEXT(p) is a set of pairs of elements of IR.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Subtype membership proofs express the domain and codomain restrictions.

claims.paraphrase: IS maps every IRI into IR ∪ IP.
claims.source_locator: Definition of a simple interpretation, numbered component 4
claims.formalization_note: There is no injectivity or unique-names requirement; different IRIs may denote the same object.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: For every IRI i, IS(i) belongs to IR union IP.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: The source IRI domain is an abstract parameter.

claims.paraphrase: IL is a partial function from literals into IR; a literal may have no denotation.
claims.source_locator: Definition of a simple interpretation, numbered component 5

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: IL is a partial function from literals to IR.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Option encodes undefinedness. It does not identify literals with their denoted values.

claims.paraphrase: A literal evaluates using IL and an IRI using IS.
claims.source_locator: Semantic conditions for ground graphs, first and second rows

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: For names, [I+A] agrees with IS on IRIs and IL on literals.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: The function is Option-valued because IL is partial.

claims.paraphrase: A ground triple is true precisely when its predicate denotes a member of IP and its subject/object denotations form a pair in that property extension; otherwise it is false.
claims.source_locator: Semantic conditions for ground graphs, third row

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: A triple s p o is true under [I+A] exactly when p denotes a property and s and o denote resources whose pair belongs to IEXT of that property.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Undefined denotation makes the existential truth condition false.

claims.paraphrase: A ground graph is true exactly when every member triple is true; one false member makes it false.
claims.source_locator: Semantic conditions for ground graphs, fourth row

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: A ground graph G is true exactly when every triple of G is true under I; no blank-node assignment is needed.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: GraphTrue also evaluates non-ground graphs under a specified A. ground_satisfaction proves agreement for ground graphs.

claims.paraphrase: A triple containing a literal with undefined IL is false, and a graph containing that triple is false.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: If IL(l) is undefined, any triple containing l in any position is false, and any graph containing that triple is false.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Covers generalized positions as well as ordinary object literals.

claims.paraphrase: The empty graph is true under every simple interpretation and remains true under conforming semantic extensions wherever their syntax admits it.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: Every simple interpretation satisfies the empty graph.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Extension preservation follows when extensions retain the same Satisfies relation and admit empty syntax.

claims.paraphrase: IP and IR may overlap. In a true triple subject/object denotations lie in IR; an IRI used as both predicate and subject/object in a true graph denotes an element of IP ∩ IR.
claims.formalization_note: The dual-role conclusion requires satisfaction of the relevant graph/triples; a false occurrence alone supplies no membership constraint.

claims.paraphrase: An extension may constrain particular IRI denotations, including fixing denotations of recognized datatype IRIs.
For an assignment A from blank nodes to IR, I+A agrees with I on names and with A on its blank-node domain; triple and graph evaluation then uses the ground rules.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: A maps exactly the blank nodes occurring in G to IR. [I+A] agrees with A on those blank nodes and with I on names.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: A partial ambient-domain function plus exact-domain condition represents the source's function on a subset. Restriction proves that unused extra assignments do not affect satisfaction.

claims.paraphrase: A graph is true under I exactly when there exists one assignment of all its blank nodes to IR that makes the entire graph true.
claims.formalization_note: The existential assignment has whole-graph scope and must be consistent across every occurrence of each blank node; per-triple independent assignments would weaken the condition.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: I satisfies G exactly when one assignment A of G's blank nodes makes every triple in G true.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: The existential assignment quantifier is outside the universal triple quantifier.

claims.paraphrase: Blank-node assignments are witnesses to graph truth rather than components of I; blank nodes have no globally fixed denotation under a simple interpretation.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: A blank-node assignment is a witness to graph truth and is not a component of the simple interpretation I.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: A structural modelling choice, not a separate theorem about all possible implementations.

claims.paraphrase: Evaluating a list through its set of triples gives the same satisfaction result after permuting or repeating identical triples, while preserving blank-node identity.
claims.formalization_note: This proves a possible set abstraction, not that list length, duplicate-returning scans, or repository APIs refine graph cardinality or unique enumeration.
